Unit 2 Seminar – EDA on the Auto-mpg dataset¶

Following the EDA tutorial, this notebook explores the Auto-mpg dataset (398 cars, model years 1970–1982). The target variable is fuel economy (mpg, miles per gallon).

Seminar tasks:

  1. Identify missing values
  2. Estimate skewness and kurtosis
  3. Correlation heat map
  4. Scatter plots for different parameters
  5. Replace categorical values with numerical values (America 1, Europe 2, …)

All figures are also saved as PNG files (2.Unit02 Auto-mpg - *.png) for the e-portfolio.

0. Setup and first look at the data¶

Handling the missing values. Only 6 of the 398 rows (1.5 %) are affected, all in horsepower. Horsepower depends strongly on engine size, so rather than using one overall mean, each missing value is filled with the median horsepower of cars with the same number of cylinders.

In [10]:
df["horsepower"] = df["horsepower"].fillna(df.groupby("cylinders")["horsepower"].transform("median"))
print("Missing values remaining:", int(df.isnull().sum().sum()))
df.loc[non_numeric.index, ["car name", "cylinders", "horsepower"]]

2. Estimate skewness and kurtosis¶

  • Skewness measures asymmetry: 0 means symmetric, > 0 means a long right tail, < 0 means a long left tail. As a rule of thumb, |skew| < 0.5 is roughly symmetric, 0.5–1 is moderately skewed and > 1 is highly skewed.
  • Kurtosis (pandas reports excess kurtosis, where a normal distribution = 0) measures how heavy the tails are. A value > 0 means more outliers than a normal distribution; < 0 means a flatter shape with lighter tails.
In [11]:
numeric = df.select_dtypes(include=np.number).drop(columns="origin")  # origin is a nominal code

def describe_skew(s):
    a = abs(s)
    shape = "approximately symmetric" if a < 0.5 else "moderately skewed" if a < 1 else "highly skewed"
    return shape + (" (right)" if s > 0.5 else " (left)" if s < -0.5 else "")

shape = pd.DataFrame({"Skewness": numeric.skew(), "Kurtosis": numeric.kurt()}).round(3)
shape["Interpretation"] = shape["Skewness"].apply(describe_skew)
shape.sort_values("Skewness", ascending=False)
Out[11]:

Does mpg follow a normal distribution? Fit the same distributions as the tutorial did for SalePrice:

In [13]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 4.5))
xs = np.linspace(df["mpg"].min(), df["mpg"].max(), 400)
for ax, (name, dist) in zip(axes, [("Johnson SU", st.johnsonsu), ("Normal", st.norm), ("Log Normal", st.lognorm)]):
    params = dist.fit(df["mpg"])
    ax.hist(df["mpg"], bins=30, density=True, alpha=0.6)
    ax.plot(xs, dist.pdf(xs, *params), "k", lw=2)
    ax.set_title(f"mpg – {name} fit")
fig.tight_layout()
save(fig, "03 mpg distribution fits")
print("Skewness of mpg:      ", round(df["mpg"].skew(), 3))
print("Skewness of log(mpg): ", round(np.log(df["mpg"]).skew(), 3))

Skewness of mpg:       0.457

3. Correlation heat map¶

origin is a nominal code (1, 2, 3 are labels, not amounts), so it is left out of the Pearson correlation matrix. cylinders and model year are ordered, so they are included.

In [14]:
corr_cols = ["mpg", "cylinders", "displacement", "horsepower", "weight", "acceleration", "model year"]
correlation = df[corr_cols].corr()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 8))
mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(correlation, dtype=bool), k=1)
sns.heatmap(correlation, mask=mask, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="coolwarm", vmin=-1, vmax=1,
            square=True, linewidths=0.5, cbar_kws={"shrink": 0.8}, ax=ax)
ax.grid(False)
ax.set_xticklabels(ax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=35, ha="right")
ax.set_yticklabels(ax.get_yticklabels(), rotation=0)
ax.set_title("Correlation heat map – Auto-mpg", fontsize=15)
save(fig, "04 correlation heatmap")

4. Scatter plots for different parameters¶

Each feature plotted against mpg, coloured by region of origin, with a linear trend line:

In [16]:
origin_names = {1: "America", 2: "Europe", 3: "Japan"}
plot_df = df.assign(region=df["origin"].map(origin_names))
palette = {"America": "#1f77b4", "Europe": "#ff7f0e", "Japan": "#2ca02c"}
regions = ["America", "Europe", "Japan"]

features = ["weight", "displacement", "horsepower", "acceleration", "model year", "cylinders"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(18, 10))
for ax, col in zip(axes.flat, features):
    sns.scatterplot(data=plot_df, x=col, y="mpg", hue="region", hue_order=regions, palette=palette, alpha=0.7, ax=ax)
    sns.regplot(data=plot_df, x=col, y="mpg", scatter=False, color="black", line_kws={"lw": 1.5}, ax=ax)
    ax.set_title(f"mpg vs {col}  (r = {df[col].corr(df['mpg']):.2f})")
fig.suptitle("Fuel economy against each feature", fontsize=15)
fig.tight_layout()
save(fig, "05 scatter mpg vs features")

Relationships between predictors (to check for multicollinearity):

In [17]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))

    ax.set_title(f"{y} vs {x}  (r = {df[x].corr(df[y]):.2f})")

g = sns.pairplot(plot_df[["mpg", "displacement", "horsepower", "weight", "acceleration", "region"]],
                 hue="region", hue_order=regions, palette=palette, diag_kind="kde", height=2.3, plot_kws={"alpha": 0.6, "s": 20})

mpg against horsepower and weight is curved, not straight: it falls steeply at first and then flattens out. A log or reciprocal transform (for example, gallons per mile = 1/mpg) straightens it out:

In [19]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))
sns.regplot(x=df["horsepower"], y=df["mpg"], order=2, scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.5}, line_kws={"color": "red"}, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title(f"mpg vs horsepower (r = {df['horsepower'].corr(df['mpg']):.2f})")
sns.regplot(x=df["horsepower"], y=1 / df["mpg"], order=2, scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.5}, line_kws={"color": "red"}, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_ylabel("1 / mpg  (gallons per mile)")
axes[1].set_title(f"1/mpg vs horsepower (r = {df['horsepower'].corr(1 / df['mpg']):.2f})")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5. Replace categorical values with numerical values¶

The dataset has two categorical variables:

Column Type Values
origin nominal already stored as codes 1/2/3 (America / Europe / Japan)
car name nominal text 305 unique names. Not usable directly; the manufacturer can be taken from the first word

5a. origin: from labels to numbers¶

To show the replacement step, origin is first written as readable labels (as it would appear in a raw data source) and then mapped back to numbers with an explicit dictionary: America → 1, Europe → 2, Japan → 3.

In [21]:
df["origin"] = df["origin"].map({1: "America", 2: "Europe", 3: "Japan"})
print("As categorical text:")
print(df["origin"].value_counts(), "\n")

origin_map = {"America": 1, "Europe": 2, "Japan": 3}
df["origin"] = df["origin"].replace(origin_map).astype(int)
print("After replacement with numbers:")
print(df["origin"].value_counts().sort_index())

As categorical text:
origin
America    249
Japan       79
Europe      70
Name: count, dtype: int64 

After replacement with numbers:
origin
1    249
2     70
3     79
Name: count, dtype: int64

5b. car name → manufacturer → numeric code¶

The first word of the car name is the manufacturer. This column contains misspellings and abbreviations (e.g. chevroelt, chevy, vw, vokswagen, toyouta, maxda), which must be fixed before encoding. Otherwise the same brand would get several different codes.

In [22]:
df["brand"] = df["car name"].str.split().str[0]
print("Raw brand spellings:", df["brand"].nunique())

brand_fixes = {
    "chevroelt": "chevrolet", "chevy": "chevrolet", "vw": "volkswagen", "vokswagen": "volkswagen",
    "toyouta": "toyota", "maxda": "mazda", "mercedes": "mercedes-benz", "capri": "mercury",
    "hi": "international harvester",
}
df["brand"] = df["brand"].replace(brand_fixes)
print("Brands after cleaning:", df["brand"].nunique())

df["brand"] = df["brand"].astype("category")
df["brand_code"] = df["brand"].cat.codes
df[["car name", "brand", "brand_code", "origin"]].sample(10, random_state=1)

5c. A note on choosing an encoding¶

Mapping categories to 1, 2, 3 (label encoding) is compact, but it suggests an order and spacing (Japan = 3 × America) that does not exist. Tree-based models handle this well. For linear models and distance-based models (k-NN, k-means), one-hot encoding is safer:

In [24]:
origin_onehot = pd.get_dummies(df["origin"].map({1: "America", 2: "Europe", 3: "Japan"}), prefix="origin", dtype=int)
pd.concat([df[["car name", "origin"]], origin_onehot], axis=1).head(8)

Summary of findings¶

1. Missing values – hidden, not absent. isnull() reports zero missing values, but horsepower contains 6 entries coded as "?" (1.5 % of rows). These placeholders also forced pandas to read the whole column as text. A missing-value check that relies only on NaN would have missed them completely. This is why data types should always be inspected during EDA. Since only six rows were affected, they were filled with the median horsepower for cars with the same cylinder count, rather than dropping the rows or using the overall mean.

2. Skewness and kurtosis.

  • horsepower is the only highly right-skewed feature (skew ≈ 1.11, kurtosis ≈ 0.75). A small number of powerful V8 cars form a long right tail.
  • displacement, weight and cylinders are moderately right-skewed (0.5–0.7), because most cars in the data are small.
  • The target mpg is only mildly skewed (0.46). After a log transform it is almost symmetric (−0.14), which helps if a linear model is used.
  • Most features have negative kurtosis, meaning flatter distributions than a normal one. cylinders (−1.38) and model year (−1.18) stand out because they are discrete and multi-modal (4, 6 and 8 cylinders), not bell-shaped.

3. Correlation heat map.

  • mpg is strongly negatively correlated with weight (−0.83), displacement (−0.80), horsepower (−0.78) and cylinders (−0.78). Heavier cars with bigger engines use more fuel.
  • mpg has a moderate positive correlation with model year (+0.58). Average mpg rose from 17.7 in 1970 to 31.7 in 1982, which reflects the oil crises and new fuel-economy regulations of that period.
  • Strong multicollinearity: cylinders, displacement, horsepower and weight correlate with each other at 0.84–0.95. In practice they all measure "engine and car size", so a linear model should keep only one or two of them (or use regularisation or PCA).

4. Scatter plots.

  • The relationship between mpg and weight or horsepower is curved: fuel economy falls quickly at first and then levels off. Using gallons per mile (1/mpg) instead makes it more linear. The correlation with horsepower rises from |−0.78| to 0.86, and with weight to 0.89.
  • Colouring by region shows clear groups. American cars are heavier and more powerful, with a median mpg of 18.5. European (26.5) and Japanese (31.6) cars are lighter, and about 90 % of them have 4 cylinders, compared with 29 % of American cars.
  • acceleration is only weakly related to mpg (+0.42) and shows a lot of scatter.

5. Categorical encoding. origin was encoded explicitly as America = 1, Europe = 2, Japan = 3. The car name column needed cleaning first: 37 raw brand spellings (e.g. chevy/chevroelt/chevrolet, vw/vokswagen/volkswagen) reduced to 29 real manufacturers, which were then label-encoded. Label codes suggest an order that does not exist (Japan is not "3 × America"). For linear or distance-based models, one-hot encoding of origin is the better choice. The fully numeric, cleaned dataset is saved as 2.Unit02 auto-mpg cleaned (numeric).csv.

Reflection. The main lesson from this exercise is that EDA is mostly about checking assumptions before trusting the data: that "no missing values" really means none, that numbers stored as text are found, that category spellings are consistent, and that strongly correlated features are not all fed into a model as if they were independent. Each of these would have quietly reduced the quality of a later model if it had been skipped.
